title: The scale of the Universe
caption: The dwarf spiral galaxy NGC 4605, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASAAcknowledgement: D. Calzetti (University of Massachusetts) and the LEGUS Team

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A bundle of bright stars and dark dust makes up this Hubble image of NGC 4605, a dwarf spiral galaxy in Ursa Major, the Great Bear. Its spiral shape is hard to see here, but it is classed as an SBc galaxy, with loose, sprawling arms and a bright bar of stars across its center.

NGC 4605 belongs to the Messier 81 group, known for unusual members, many formed in galaxy collisions. With its somewhat odd shape, NGC 4605 fits the family, though the origin of its quirks is not yet clear.

Astronomers use it as a testing ground. Its young stars help show how interactions affect the birth and life of stars, and how stellar nurseries gather into clusters. It is also a test for dark matter, since the way dark matter seems to be spread through its halo does not quite match what models predict, though the evidence is still inconclusive.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this data are invisible to the eye.

explore: Few galaxy groups lie closer to our own Local Group than the Messier 81 group. Both belong to the Virgo Supercluster, a collection of some 100 groups and clusters. The caption places NGC 4605 around 16 million light-years away.
alt: A compact galaxy of bright stars and dark dust without an obvious spiral shape.
